statement: The Rothschilds were behind the Federal Reserve, and they now control the global financial system.
label: false

what: were behind the Federal Reserve, and they now control the global financial system

prompt: Why The Rothschilds were behind the Federal Reserve, and they now control the global financial system?
answer:
Short answer: There’s no reliable evidence that the Rothschild family created the U.S. Federal Reserve or that they control the global financial system. The historical record and the Fed’s own legal structure show otherwise.

What the record shows
- How the Fed was created: Congress passed, and President Woodrow Wilson signed, the Federal Reserve Act on December 23, 1913, establishing the Federal Reserve as the U.S. central bank to address recurrent banking panics. ([federalreservehistory.org](https://www.federalreservehistory.org/-/media/Project/FedHistory/FedHistory/Documents/essaysPDFs/Federal-Reserve-Act-Signed-into-Law-_-Federal-Reserve-History.pdf))
- Who designed it: A 1910 drafting meeting at Jekyll Island involved Senator Nelson Aldrich, A. Piatt Andrew (Treasury official), Henry Davison (J.P. Morgan & Co.), Frank Vanderlip (National City Bank), Arthur Shelton (Aldrich’s secretary), and banker Paul Warburg. No Rothschild family members were present. ([federalreservehistory.org](https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/jekyll-island-conference))
- Who “owns” and governs the Fed: The Board of Governors in Washington, D.C., is a federal agency; its seven members are nominated by the U.S. President and confirmed by the Senate. Monetary policy is set by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), composed of the Governors plus Reserve Bank presidents. Regional Reserve Banks issue non‑tradable stock to member banks by law, but the System is not “owned” by any family or outside group, and Reserve Banks are not run for profit; after expenses and limited dividends, net earnings are remitted to the U.S. Treasury. ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/faqs/about_14986.htm))
- Independent checks and public accountability: The Fed reports to Congress, publishes audited financial statements, and its policy decisions do not require approval by the President or Congress—standard features intended to insulate monetary policy from day‑to‑day politics, not to place it under private control. ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/faqs/about_14986.htm))

About the “global control” claim
- Central banks around the world are public institutions or statutory authorities. The Bank for International Settlements (BIS)—often cited in conspiracy claims—is owned exclusively by member central banks (since 2001, private shareholders have been excluded). It is not owned or run by private families. ([bis.org](https://www.bis.org/about/member_cb.htm?utm_source=openai))
- Reputable fact‑checkers have repeatedly found no evidence that the Rothschilds own the Fed or control central banks worldwide; such claims recycle long‑running conspiracy theories. ([politifact.com](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/mar/01/facebook-posts/rothschild-conspiracy-theory-resurfaces-but-family/?utm_source=openai))

Why the rumor persists
- The Rothschilds were a prominent European banking dynasty in the 19th century, which makes them a frequent target of exaggerated or false claims. That historical prominence is not evidence of present‑day control over the Fed or the global financial system. ([britannica.com](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Rothschild-family?utm_source=openai))

Conclusion
Based on primary sources and reputable analyses, the statement “The Rothschilds were behind the Federal Reserve, and they now control the global financial system” is not supported by credible evidence. ([federalreserve.gov](https://www.federalreserve.gov/faqs/about_14986.htm))

statement: United Nations troops can 'round up' and forcibly 'vaccinate the population' if WHO pandemic treaty is passed.

subject: Government and Political Entities
prompt: Why United Nations troops can 'round up' and forcibly 'vaccinate the population' if WHO pandemic treaty is passed?
answer:
Short answer: They can’t. Neither the WHO’s pandemic agreement nor the International Health Regulations (IHR) give the WHO, the UN, or “UN troops” any power to enter countries and forcibly vaccinate people.

What the new WHO Pandemic Agreement actually says
- The agreement, adopted by the World Health Assembly on May 20, 2025, explicitly reaffirms national sovereignty and states that it does not give WHO authority to mandate domestic measures such as vaccination mandates or lockdowns. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/news/item/20-05-2025-world-health-assembly-adopts-historic-pandemic-agreement-to-make-the-world-more-equitable-and-safer-from-future-pandemics?utm_source=openai))

What legal authority the WHO has (and does not have)
- The WHO issues technical guidance and, under the IHR, only non-binding “temporary” or “standing” recommendations to countries. It cannot compel a country to adopt a vaccine mandate or any other domestic policy. ([apps.who.int](https://apps.who.int/gb/bd/pdf_files/IHR_2022-en.pdf?utm_source=openai))
- The IHR also require that health measures respect human rights, including dignity and informed consent. ([apps.who.int](https://apps.who.int/gb/bd/pdf_files/IHR_2022-en.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Why the UN cannot “send in troops” to enforce vaccination
- The UN has no standing army. Peacekeepers are personnel contributed by member states and can be deployed only when the UN Security Council authorizes a mission—typically with the host country’s consent—and to address threats to international peace and security, not to run national health programs. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council?utm_source=openai))
- The WHO is a specialized UN agency; it does not control peacekeeping forces and cannot order any military deployment. ([peacekeeping.un.org](https://peacekeeping.un.org/en/node/8007?utm_source=openai))

Status of the IHR (separate from the Pandemic Agreement)
- Targeted amendments to the IHR were adopted in 2024 and entered into force on September 19, 2025. They strengthen coordination and reporting but do not grant WHO enforcement powers over countries. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/news/item/19-09-2025-amended-international-health-regulations-enter-into-force?utm_source=openai))

Independent fact-checks
- Repeated social media claims that a WHO treaty would allow UN troops to “round up” people for forced vaccination have been rated false by multiple fact-checkers. ([politifact.com](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2024/jan/26/instagram-posts/pandemic-treaty-wouldnt-give-the-who-power-to-forc/?utm_source=openai))

If you want, I can point you to the specific treaty and IHR clauses so you can read the exact language yourself.

statement: China is in a situation where they have more retired than working.
label: false
speaker: Joe Biden
true_statement: Does China have more retirees than workers? Joe Biden’s claim is premature
what: is in a situation where they have more retired than working
subject: Government and Political Entities
prompt: Why China is in a situation where they have more retired than working?
answer:
Short answer
China does not currently have “more retired than working.” As of December 31, 2023, people aged 60+ were about 297 million (21.1% of the population), and those aged 16–59 were about 865 million (61.3%); the number of employed people was about 740 million. What is happening is a rapid shift toward an older age structure, which raises the old‑age dependency ratio (older people relative to the working‑age population). ([stats.gov.cn](https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202402/t20240228_1947918.html?os=ios))

Why the shift is happening
- Prolonged very low fertility. Births fell to 9.02 million in 2023, and China’s fertility has been well below the “replacement” level of 2.1 children per woman for years, contributing to a shrinking younger cohort. UN estimates place China among the world’s ultra‑low‑fertility countries. ([stats.gov.cn](https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202402/t20240228_1947918.html?os=ios))
- Rapid gains in longevity and large cohorts entering retirement. Life expectancy is around 78 years, and the share aged 65+ reached about 15% in 2023, pushing up the number of retirees. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2024/12/pensions-at-a-glance-asia-pacific-2024_fcc7bc58/d4146d12-en.pdf))
- Earlier family‑planning policies compressed the size of younger generations. The one‑child policy (ended in 2015) was followed by a two‑child policy in 2016 and a three‑child policy in 2021, but these shifts have not reversed the low‑fertility trend. ([loc.gov](https://www.loc.gov/item/global-legal-monitor/2016-01-08/china-two-child-policy-becomes-law/?utm_source=openai))
- The working‑age population has been declining for over a decade. Official data showed the first sustained drop around 2011–2012, and the working‑age share has continued to edge down since. ([stats.gov.cn](https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/201201/t20120120_72112.html?utm_source=openai))
- Relatively low statutory retirement ages increase the number counted as “retired.” (Historically 60 for men; 50–55 for women, depending on job.) China has now decided to raise these ages gradually from 2025 over 15 years to ease pressure from population aging. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2024/12/pensions-at-a-glance-asia-pacific-2024_fcc7bc58/d4146d12-en.pdf))
- Social and economic factors discourage marriage and child‑rearing. Marriage registrations have fallen to record lows in recent years, and most births occur within marriage in China, further weighing on future births. ([usa.chinadaily.com.cn](https://usa.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202306/12/WS64868056a31033ad3f7bbbd0.html?utm_source=openai))

What the numbers imply
- China’s old‑age dependency ratio is now above 20 older persons (65+) per 100 working‑age people and is projected to rise sharply in coming decades, even though today’s workers still far outnumber retirees. ([oecd.org](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2024/12/pensions-at-a-glance-asia-pacific-2024_fcc7bc58/d4146d12-en.pdf))

In short: China doesn’t yet have more retirees than workers, but decades of low fertility, rising longevity, past family‑planning policies, and low retirement ages have created a fast‑aging population and a shrinking workforce. Authorities are responding (for example, by gradually raising retirement ages), but demographic momentum means the old‑age burden will keep rising for years. ([stats.gov.cn](https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202402/t20240228_1947918.html?os=ios))

Short answer: Congress does not prohibit the NIH from researching the causes of mass shootings. What federal law restricts is using NIH (and other HHS) funds to advocate or promote gun control, not to conduct scientific research.

Key facts
- The “Dickey Amendment” language, first applied to CDC funding in 1996 and later extended across HHS (including NIH), says appropriated funds “may not be used, in whole or in part, to advocate or promote gun control.” It does not ban research. In 2018, Congress explicitly noted that CDC has authority to research the causes of gun violence notwithstanding the rider. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF11371))
- In December 2019 (FY2020), Congress for the first time in decades appropriated dedicated federal funding—$25 million split between CDC and NIH—for firearm‑injury research; subsequent appropriations have continued NIH support. ([abcnews.go.com](https://abcnews.go.com/Health/congress-approves-unprecedented-25-million-gun-violence-research/story?id=67762555&utm_source=openai))

What this means today
- NIH can and does fund research on firearm injury and mortality prevention (which can include studying mass shootings and their risk factors), provided the work is scientific and not advocacy. The restriction is on advocacy, not on studying causes. ([grants.nih.gov](https://grants.nih.gov/grants/policy/nihgps/HTML5/section%204/4.2.3%20gun%20control.htm?utm_source=openai))

Why the misconception exists
- For many years, agencies—particularly CDC—reduced firearms research because the rider and related budget actions created a chilling effect, even though the statute itself targets advocacy. Congress and the executive branch have since clarified that research is allowed, and Congress has reestablished dedicated funding. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF11371))

statement: Adolf Heusinger was Adolf Hitler’s chief of staff and after World War II ended became the chief of staff for NATO forces.
label: half-true
what: was Adolf Hitler’s chief of staff and after World War II ended became the chief of staff for NATO forces
subject: Public Figures
prompt: Why Adolf Heusinger was Adolf Hitler’s chief of staff and after World War II ended became the chief of staff for NATO forces?
answer:
Short answer
- Heusinger was not “Hitler’s chief of staff.” In World War II he was a career staff officer who headed the Operations Section of the Army High Command (OKH) from 1940–1944 and regularly briefed Hitler; he was briefly wounded in the 20 July 1944 bomb attack and then held by the Gestapo. He was never convicted of war crimes and, after denazification, worked for U.S. authorities. In the Cold War, West Germany rearmed and integrated into NATO; Heusinger helped build the new Bundeswehr, became its first Inspector General (1957–1961), and then served as Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee (1961–1964). NATO does not have a single “chief of staff”; the Military Committee’s chair is the Alliance’s senior military adviser, not a commander of NATO forces. ([kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de](https://kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de/resources/pdf/f2828cdb-3d32-4d88-9fb3-223632ef3547.pdf))

Why this happened (with sources)
- His wartime role was professional staff work, not Hitler’s personal staff: Heusinger led the OKH Operationsabteilung (operations section) from 1940, placing him in the army’s senior planning circle and at regular Lage (situation) conferences with Hitler. He was injured in the 20 July 1944 explosion and then briefly held by the Gestapo. ([kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de](https://kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de/resources/pdf/f2828cdb-3d32-4d88-9fb3-223632ef3547.pdf))
- Post‑war screening and U.S. use: After 1945 he was a U.S. prisoner of war, then served as a witness/expert for U.S. war‑crimes proceedings and worked in the U.S. Army Historical Division; in 1948 he became head of analysis in the CIA‑supervised Gehlen Organization. In denazification he was classified “affected, but not incriminated” (betroffen, aber nicht belastet). These factors made him employable in West German and Allied institutions. ([deutsche-biographie.de](https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/dbo067347.html?language=en))
- West German rearmament and integration into NATO: As Bonn decided to rearm within the Western alliance, Heusinger advised Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, took part in the 1950 Himmerod conference on building new forces, and rose to be the Bundeswehr’s first Inspector General (1957–1961). His experience and political reliability in the eyes of the West led to his selection as Chairman of NATO’s Military Committee (1961–1964). ([kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de](https://kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de/resources/pdf/f2828cdb-3d32-4d88-9fb3-223632ef3547.pdf))
- What his NATO job actually was: NATO’s own record shows Heusinger chaired the Military Committee in Permanent Session (1961–1963) and then the Military Committee (1963–1964). The chair is NATO’s senior military adviser to the Secretary General; it is not a “chief of staff for NATO forces.” ([nato.int](https://www.nato.int/en/about-us/organization/who-we-are/chairs-of-the-military-committee))

Key dates to clarify the timeline
- 1940–1944: Chief, OKH Operations Section; attended Hitler’s situation conferences. Injured on July 20, 1944; briefly in Gestapo custody. ([kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de](https://kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de/resources/pdf/f2828cdb-3d32-4d88-9fb3-223632ef3547.pdf))
- 1947–1950: With U.S. Army Historical Division; 1948–1951: Head of analysis, Gehlen Organization. Denazification: “affected, not incriminated.” ([deutsche-biographie.de](https://www.deutsche-biographie.de/dbo067347.html?language=en))
- 1957–1961: First Inspector General of the Bundeswehr (highest-ranking officer). ([kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de](https://kabinettsprotokolle.bundesarchiv.de/resources/pdf/f2828cdb-3d32-4d88-9fb3-223632ef3547.pdf))
- 1961–1964: Chairman, NATO Military Committee (Permanent Session 1961–1963; Military Committee 1963–1964). ([nato.int](https://www.nato.int/en/about-us/organization/who-we-are/chairs-of-the-military-committee))

In sum: Heusinger advanced in NATO-era roles not because he had been “Hitler’s chief of staff,” but because (a) he was a senior but unconvicted Wehrmacht staff officer, (b) he was employed by U.S. authorities after the war, and (c) West Germany’s rearmament and integration into NATO required experienced leadership—leading to his appointment as Bundeswehr Inspector General and later NATO Military Committee Chair. Gates has been a donor to academic research programs that study solar geoengineering as a risk‑management option for climate change. In 2024, the New York Court of Appeals dismissed the appeal, and in 2025 it denied leave, leaving the Appellate Division’s standing dismissal in place; there was no high‑court ruling on the regulation’s substance. (law.justia.com; nycourts.gov)

Important context in New York law
- Long before COVID‑19, New York Public Health Law § 2120 (enacted in 1953) has allowed a health officer to seek a court order—after notice and a hearing—to commit a person with a communicable disease to a hospital or institution if the person is found to be a “menace to others.” That statute, not § 2.13, is where any court‑ordered confinement authority comes from. (nysenate.gov)

Bottom line: The “quarantine camps and imprisonment” claim is not supported by reliable sources. The disputed rule was an administrative public‑health procedure with due‑process provisions; it did not create new criminal penalties or detention “camps,” although it permitted quarantine at congregate facilities and referenced that existing civil or criminal penalties could apply for violating public‑health orders. statement: Donald Trump ran up more debt than any other president in American history
label: mostly-false
speaker: Hakeem Jeffries
true_statement: Did Donald Trump rack up more debt than any other president?
what: ran up more debt than any other president in American history
subject: Government and Political Entities
prompt: Why Donald Trump ran up more debt than any other president in American history?
answer:
Short answer
Measured in raw dollars over a single four‑year term, Donald Trump presided over the largest increase in the national debt on record: gross federal debt rose by about $7.8 trillion (and debt held by the public by about $7.2 trillion) between January 2017 and January 2021. That “largest ever in any four years” result reflects both emergency borrowing during COVID‑19 and policy choices that widened deficits before the pandemic. ([factcheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2023/02/factchecking-the-state-of-the-union-4/?utm_source=openai))

What drove the increase
- Pandemic shock and relief: The 2020 recession cut revenues and triggered very large bipartisan aid packages. The CARES Act (March 2020), the December 2020 Response & Relief Act, and other COVID laws together accounted for roughly $3.6 trillion of ten‑year borrowing impact; they also produced the record $3.1 trillion deficit in FY2020. ([crfb.org](https://www.crfb.org/papers/trump-and-biden-national-debt)) ([cbo.gov](https://www.cbo.gov/system/files/2020-04/hr748.pdf?utm_source=openai)) ([crfb.org](https://www.crfb.org/papers/trump-and-biden-national-debt))
- 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA): The law reduced revenues; official scorers projected substantial deficit increases over a decade. CRFB’s synthesis attributes about $1.9 trillion of ten‑year debt to TCJA, and CRS notes no mainstream model finds that the law “paid for itself.” ([crfb.org](https://www.crfb.org/papers/trump-and-biden-national-debt)) ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48485?utm_source=openai))
- Higher discretionary spending caps: The Bipartisan Budget Acts of 2018 and 2019 lifted the Budget Control Act caps (by a combined $296 billion for 2018–2019 and $320 billion for 2020–2021), leading CRFB to attribute about $2.1 trillion of ten‑year debt to those deals. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/72/Congressional_Budget_Office_report_2019-02-27_-_Testimony_on_Discretionary_Appropriations_Under_the_Budget_Control_Act.pdf?utm_source=openai)) ([crfb.org](https://www.crfb.org/papers/trump-and-biden-national-debt))
- Other policy choices: Congress and the administration also delayed/repealed several ACA taxes and took health‑policy actions that raised federal costs, which CRFB tallies at roughly $1.0 trillion combined over ten years (including interest). Tariff increases partially offset this (on paper) by several hundred billion over ten years. ([crfb.org](https://www.crfb.org/papers/trump-and-biden-national-debt))

Important context
- Shared responsibility: Major drivers above were enacted by Congress (often on bipartisan votes) and signed by the President; budget outcomes reflect both branches. ([crfb.org](https://www.crfb.org/papers/trump-and-biden-national-debt))
- Measurement matters: The “most ever” claim pertains to any four‑year span in nominal dollars. By other yardsticks the picture changes: for example, Obama oversaw a larger eight‑year dollar increase, and several earlier presidents saw bigger jumps relative to GDP. ([factcheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2023/02/factchecking-the-state-of-the-union-4/?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line
Trump’s record four‑year dollar increase mainly reflects (1) emergency COVID‑19 borrowing and (2) pre‑pandemic policy choices—tax cuts and higher discretionary caps—that expanded deficits atop already‑rising structural pressures. ([crfb.org](https://www.crfb.org/papers/trump-and-biden-national-debt))

Short answer: It didn’t. - What changed: On March 31, 2023, the Pentagon comptroller re‑issued guidance clarifying that drawdown items must be valued at net book value, not replacement cost. - The effect: Because the earlier totals had been overstated, DoD had that much more drawdown authority remaining without new congressional appropriations. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/716ce5f7f336f1def7e000ac9170f190?utm_source=openai))

Because access to the types of guns most often used in school attacks was made extremely difficult, and remaining legal access to any firearm is tightly vetted and monitored. Since the 1996 Dunblane massacre, Great Britain banned private handgun ownership and paired that with rigorous licensing, secure‑storage rules, and active enforcement that together leave very few pathways for would‑be school shooters to obtain and keep firearms. ([britannica.com](https://www.britannica.com/question/How-did-British-gun-laws-change-after-the-Dunblane-massacre?utm_source=openai))
- Tight licensing for any remaining legal firearms (mainly shotguns and rifles): Applicants must show “good reason,” pass police background checks and home visits, meet security requirements (e.g., BS 7558‑standard locked cabinets), and can be refused on suitability grounds. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/statutory-guidance-for-police-on-firearms-licensing/firearms-licensing-statutory-guidance-for-chief-officers-of-police-accessible?utm_source=openai))
- Ongoing tightening after later tragedies: Following the 2021 Plymouth shootings with a licensed shotgun, the government issued/updated statutory guidance and consulted on further changes; police forces were told to re‑review licences and strengthen vetting and training. - Low legal prevalence and active oversight: Around 497,000 people in England and Wales held a firearm or shotgun certificate as of March 2025 (in a population of ~60+ million), and the police have broad discretion to refuse or revoke. Secure‑storage inspections are part of the regime. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/firearm-and-shotgun-certificates-april-2024-to-march-2025/firearm-and-shotgun-certificates-april-2024-to-march-2025?utm_source=openai))

statement: COVID-19 vaccines can slightly alter menstrual cycle temporarily, but don’t harm fertility.
label: true
what: can slightly alter menstrual cycle temporarily, but don’t harm fertility
subject: Miscellaneous
prompt: Why COVID-19 vaccines can slightly alter menstrual cycle temporarily, but don’t harm fertility?
answer:
Short answer
- Immune activation from vaccination can temporarily shift the hormones and local immune signals that coordinate a menstrual cycle, so some people see a small, short‑lived change in timing or flow. Large, well‑done studies show these shifts average less than a day (about two days if two doses fall in the same cycle) and return to baseline within one or two cycles. ([bmjmedicine.bmj.com](https://bmjmedicine.bmj.com/content/1/1/e000297?utm_source=openai))
- By contrast, multiple high‑quality studies in people trying to conceive, in IVF clinics, and in hormone testing show COVID‑19 vaccination does not reduce fertility or increase miscarriage risk. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/aje/article/191/8/1383/6511811?utm_source=openai))

What we know about periods after vaccination
- Magnitude and duration: App‑based cohort studies funded by NIH found a small average increase in cycle length during the cycle(s) when a dose is received (under one day on average; roughly two days if two doses occur in the same cycle). Cycles returned to usual length by the next one or two cycles; menses length did not change. ([bmjmedicine.bmj.com](https://bmjmedicine.bmj.com/content/1/1/e000297?utm_source=openai))
- Timing matters: A newer analysis indicates the effect is mainly when vaccination occurs in the follicular (first) half of the cycle, consistent with a transient shift in the hormonal signals that set ovulation timing. ([nichd.nih.gov](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/newsroom/news/022924-COVID-19-vaccination-menstrual-cycle?utm_source=openai))
- Symptoms: An NIH‑funded study also found a small increase in the proportion reporting heavier‑than‑usual bleeding after the first dose; most did not report changes in regularity, bleed length, or menstrual pain. ([nichd.nih.gov](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/newsroom/news/041023-COVID-19-vaccination-menstrual-cycle?utm_source=openai))

Why this can happen (biological plausibility)
- The endometrium is an immune‑active tissue; cytokines and immune cells fluctuate across the cycle and help regulate endometrial shedding and repair. A brisk, short‑term immune response to vaccination can transiently interact with this system and with the hypothalamic‑pituitary‑ovarian axis, nudging cycle timing without lasting effects. ([rbej.biomedcentral.com](https://rbej.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1477-7827-1-116?utm_source=openai))
- Supporting clue: the follicular‑phase sensitivity noted above fits a temporary influence on ovulatory timing rather than on uterine structure or long‑term ovarian function. ([nichd.nih.gov](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/newsroom/news/022924-COVID-19-vaccination-menstrual-cycle?utm_source=openai))

Why vaccines don’t harm fertility
- Time‑to‑pregnancy (natural conception): A large prospective cohort following more than 2,000 U.S. and Canadian couples found no reduction in fecundability (chance of conception per cycle) in vaccinated women or men. Notably, SARS‑CoV‑2 infection (not vaccination) in male partners was linked to a short‑term dip in fecundability. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/aje/article/191/8/1383/6511811?utm_source=openai))
- IVF outcomes: Studies from IVF programs (including JAMA Network Open analyses) show no differences in ovarian stimulation metrics, fertilization, embryo quality, implantation, or pregnancy rates between vaccinated and unvaccinated patients, including across different vaccine types and intervals. ([jamanetwork.com](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2791457?utm_source=openai))
- Ovarian reserve: Multiple studies measuring anti‑Müllerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle count before and after vaccination show no meaningful changes, arguing against any depletion of ovarian reserve. ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/humrep/article/37/3/534/6478280?utm_source=openai))
- Miscarriage and pregnancy safety: CDC analyses of the v‑safe pregnancy registry and related cohorts have not found increased miscarriage risk after mRNA vaccination, and preconception vaccination was not associated with miscarriage in a 2023 Human Reproduction cohort. ([archive.cdc.gov](https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/media/releases/2021/s0811-vaccine-safe-pregnant.html?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line
- Brief, mild menstrual changes after COVID‑19 vaccination are a known, temporary effect of immune activation and cycle timing and typically resolve quickly. Robust evidence from cohort studies, IVF clinics, hormone testing, and CDC surveillance shows COVID‑19 vaccines do not impair fertility or raise miscarriage risk. If bleeding is very heavy, lasts much longer than usual, or you miss three periods in a row, seek medical advice to rule out other causes. ([bmjmedicine.bmj.com](https://bmjmedicine.bmj.com/content/1/1/e000297?utm_source=openai))

- What the bill did: H.R. 4760 created a renewable, three‑year “contingent nonimmigrant” status for a subset of DACA recipients (no citizenship track) and bundled it with E‑Verify expansion, legal‑immigration cuts, and significant border‑security funding. prompt: Why New York City is spraying unsafe pesticides to combat West Nile virus?
answer:
Short answer
New York City sprays pesticides when its mosquito surveillance shows a heightened risk of West Nile virus to people. Spraying is one part of an integrated program that prioritizes eliminating standing water and larviciding; adulticide truck spraying is used selectively, at night, in areas with documented risk. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/wnv/2024/wnvplan2024.pdf))

What the City is using
- Adulticides: Anvil 10+10 (d‑phenothrin/sumithrin with piperonyl butoxide), Duet (pyrethroids), and Merus 3.0 (pyrethrins). Larvicides include bacterial products such as VectoBac (Bti) and VectoLex (Ls). These products are registered for public‑health mosquito control and are the formulations listed by NYC for the 2024–2025 seasons. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray-2024.page))

Why public‑health officials spray
- West Nile virus has been detected in NYC mosquitoes every year since 1999, and it can cause severe neurologic disease and death; there is no human vaccine. In 2025 the City recorded multiple neuroinvasive WNV cases. Spraying helps quickly reduce infectious adult mosquito populations when surveillance indicates elevated risk. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray.page))

Is the spraying “unsafe”?
- According to NYC Health and the U.S. EPA, when these pesticides are applied as ultra‑low‑volume sprays according to their labels, they are not expected to pose significant health risks to the general population. NYC notes some sensitive people may experience short‑term eye, throat, or skin irritation and advises simple precautions (e.g., staying indoors during spraying, using recirculate on AC). ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray.page))
- EPA’s human‑health reviews of commonly used mosquito adulticides (pyrethroids/pyrethrins, including sumithrin) conclude they can be used for public‑health mosquito control “without posing unreasonable risks” when label directions are followed; EPA has added mitigation measures to address ecological concerns such as spray drift and risks to aquatic organisms and pollinators. ([epa.gov](https://www.epa.gov/mosquitocontrol/permethrin-resmethrin-d-phenothrin-sumithrinr-synthetic-pyrethroids-mosquito?utm_source=openai))

How decisions are made and when spraying happens
- NYC’s Comprehensive Mosquito Surveillance and Control Plan specifies that adulticiding is triggered by data (positive mosquito pools, species, persistence, season, proximity to people). Applications are done in the evening or early morning to limit human and pollinator exposure, with public notice at least 24 hours in advance. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/wnv/2024/wnvplan2024.pdf))

If you’re concerned about exposure
- You can sign up for spray notifications, stay indoors during operations, and report standing water so the City can remove breeding sites—steps NYC Health explicitly recommends. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray.page))

Bottom line
NYC sprays not because it seeks to expose residents to “unsafe” chemicals, but because surveillance shows a real, recurring risk from West Nile virus. The products used are EPA‑registered and, per NYC Health and EPA, are considered low risk when applied properly, though simple precautions are advised and ecological safeguards are required. ([nyc.gov](https://www.nyc.gov/site/doh/health/health-topics/west-nile-virus-spray.page))

subject: Government and Political Entities
prompt: Why Gov. Ron DeSantis actually sponsored the bill to make Puerto Rico a state?
answer:
Short answer: He didn’t sponsor the bill; he co‑sponsored it as a U.S. representative in 2018. The lead sponsor was Puerto Rico’s Resident Commissioner Jenniffer González‑Colón.

What we can verify with high confidence:
- Role and bill: DeSantis was an original co‑sponsor of H.R. 6246 (Puerto Rico Admission Act of 2018), introduced on June 27, 2018, which outlined a transition process culminating in Puerto Rico’s admission “no later than January 1, 2021” after a congressional task force reported and a presidential proclamation was issued. ([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/bill/115th-congress/house-bill/6246/cosponsors))
- Rationale he (via his campaign) offered later: In 2023 his campaign said the 2018 bill “didn’t grant or take a position on Puerto Rican statehood; it clarified the process by which statehood would be granted to ensure it was subject to the will of the American people and a full congressional vote.” ([politifact.com](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2023/nov/01/maga-inc/ron-desantis-in-2018-backed-a-bill-drafting-a-path/))
- Context at the time: The bill had bipartisan backing (58 co‑sponsors, including 12 from Florida). Florida was home to roughly 1.1 million Puerto Ricans, and both parties were courting those voters after Hurricane Maria. While running for governor in June 2018, DeSantis told the Associated Press he would “take the case to the Puerto Rican community,” calling them “natural Republicans.” These facts show the political salience of Puerto Rico issues in Florida in 2018, though they do not by themselves prove his personal motive for co‑sponsoring. ([politifact.com](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2023/nov/01/maga-inc/ron-desantis-in-2018-backed-a-bill-drafting-a-path/))
- Party platform backdrop: Support for Puerto Rico statehood (if Puerto Ricans want it) has appeared in Republican Party platforms for decades (e.g., 1940’s platform called statehood a “logical aspiration”). ([presidency.ucsb.edu](https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/republican-party-platform-1940))

Bottom line: The verifiable record is that DeSantis, as a House member, joined a large bipartisan group backing H.R. 6246’s statehood process. His campaign’s stated reasoning is that the bill was about clarifying a voter‑driven process subject to Congress. Beyond those on‑the‑record points, I don’t have sufficient reliable information to confirm any additional, specific personal motive. ([politifact.com](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2023/nov/01/maga-inc/ron-desantis-in-2018-backed-a-bill-drafting-a-path/))
